query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: The use of laser powder bed fusion with optimized process parameters and in-situ alloy formation will result in improved mechanical properties, reduced residual thermal stresses, and increased relative density (>98%) compared to conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing conditions, by forming a single-phase solid solution with refined grain structure through in-situ alloy formation and rapid solidification during laser powder bed fusion.
generation.intervention: Laser powder bed fusion with optimized process parameters and in-situ alloy formation
generation.conditions: Volumetric energy density (VED) window of 50 J/mm3 to 83 J/mm3, layer thickness of 20-50 μm, and scanning speed of 100-500 mm/s, with optimized VED settings to minimize titanium evaporation
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a single-phase solid solution with refined grain structure
generation.mechanism: In-situ alloy formation and rapid solidification during laser powder bed fusion, leading to the formation of a nonequilibrium chemical short-range order
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical properties, reduced residual thermal stresses, and increased relative density (>98%) compared to conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing conditions
generation.boundary: The optimized process parameters and VED settings will be within the range of 50 J/mm3 to 83 J/mm3, and the layer thickness and scanning speed will be within the range of 20-50 μm and 100-500 mm/s, respectively
generation.uncertainty: The potential risk of evaporation loss of titanium at higher VED settings, and the need for further optimization of the VED settings to minimize titanium evaporation while maintaining the desired microstructure and mechanical properties

falsification_experiment.design: A comparative study of the mechanical properties and microstructure of AlCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy samples fabricated using laser powder bed fusion with optimized process parameters and in-situ alloy formation, and conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples fabricated using laser powder bed fusion with optimized process parameters and in-situ alloy formation do not exhibit improved mechanical properties and reduced residual thermal stresses compared to the samples fabricated using conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys are known for their promising mechanical properties, wear and corrosion resistance, which are maintained across a wide range of temperatures. In this study, a CoCrFeNiCu-based high-entropy alloy, distinguished from conventional CoCrFeNi systems by the addition of Cu, which is known to enhance toughness and wear resistance, was investigated to better understand the effects of compositional modification on processability and performance. The influence of key process parameters, specifically laser power and scan speed, on the processability of CoCrFeNiCu-based high-entropy alloys produced by laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing was investigated, with a focus of low laser power, which is critical for minimizing defects and improving the resulting microstructure and mechanical performance. The printed sample density gradually increases with higher volumetric energy density, achieving densities exceeding 99.0%. However, at higher energy densities, the samples exhibit susceptibility to hot cracking, an issue that cannot be mitigated by adjusting the process parameters. Mechanical properties under optimized parameters were further evaluated using Charp

The synthesis of HEA WTaMoNbV via the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder was demonstrated as feasible because of its similar microstructure, physical properties and electrochemical behavior compared to its counterpart alloy produced by the conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) process. In both cases, the alloys were composed of a single solid phase solution, with a BCC crystal structure with similar lattice parameters. Further experimental work is needed to continue to optimize the printing parameters of the LPBF process along with possible a post-heat-treatment process to rectify inherent printing defects.

High entropy alloys (HEAs) and their closely related variants, called multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), are the topic of a rather new area of research, and so far, the gathered knowledge is incomplete. This is especially true when it comes to material libraries, as the fabrication of HEA and MPEA samples with a wide variation in chemical compositions is challenging in itself. Additive manufacturing technologies are, to date, seen as possibly the best option to quickly fabricate HEA and MPEA samples, offering both the melting metallurgical and solid-state sintering approach. Within this study, CrFeNiTi MPEA samples were fabricated via laser powder-bed fusion (PBF-LB) and solid-state sintering of mechanically alloyed powder feedstock. The main emphasis is on the PBF-LB process, while solid-state sintering serves as benchmark. Within a volumetric energy density (VED) window of 50 J/mm3 to 83 J/mm3, dense samples with large defect-free sections and an average micro-hardness of 965 HV0.1 were fabricated. decision.rationale: The intervention proposed in direction A, laser powder bed fusion with optimized process parameters and in-situ alloy formation, directly addresses the limitations of mainstream metallic additive manufacturing regimes by reducing residual thermal stresses, improving mechanical properties, and increasing relative density.
